title: Construction Laborers

claims.text: Safe Work Australia confirms Australia will adopt the Workplace Exposure Limits for Airborne Contaminants (WEL list) from 1 December 2026, replacing the Workplace Exposure Standards (WES list) after WHS ministers agreed to a harmonised transition implemented into the WHS laws of the Commonwealth, states and territories; the change covers respirable crystalline silica among other contaminants.

sources.title: Workplace Exposure Limits - airborne contaminants
sources.whatItMeasured: Official statement of the WES-to-WEL transition date (1 December 2026) and the WHS ministers' agreement, as the binding exposure-standard instrument

claims.scope: All airborne contaminants, including respirable crystalline silica. Binding exposure-standard change that sets the lawful dust-exposure ceiling for construction and demolition labourers; it is not an employment, automation or wage instrument.
claims.refuteNotes: Lens 1 (source real): statutory national work-health body, page resolves HTTP 200 and is the authoritative transition statement. Lens 2 (population fit): applies to any worker exposed to airborne contaminants including labourers on dusty construction/demolition tasks. Lens 3 (in window): transition dated 1 December 2026, announced/active in 2026, inside window. No refuter overturned.

claims.text: The Australian Centre for Disease Control (CDC) published updated national guidance on 1 July 2026 stating that around 4% of Australian workers are at risk of exposure to respirable crystalline silica across construction, demolition, tunnelling, mining, masonry and engineered stone, with researchers estimating current workplace exposure could lead to more than 83,000 future cases; it reaffirms the 2024 nationwide ban on the importation and use of engineered stone.

sources.title: Updated national guidance helps doctors protect Aussie workers from silica dust
sources.whatItMeasured: Government health-agency release on updated clinical guidance, the share of workers exposed to silica, and the projected future case burden

claims.scope: Health-professional guidance and disease-burden estimates, not a new binding instrument. Relevant to construction labourers because cutting, grinding and demolition generate silica dust; the 2024 engineered-stone ban predates the window and is noted only as background.
claims.refuteNotes: Lens 1 (source real): official Australian CDC news page, resolves HTTP 200, dated 1 July 2026. Lens 2 (population fit): construction and demolition are named exposure industries, so the 4% / 83,000 figures include this occupation. Lens 3 (in window): July 2026, inside window. Dissent recorded: the 83,000 figure is a forward estimate from researchers, not a confirmed case count.

claims.text: 2026 rate cards for Australian construction labour classify a CW1 General Construction Labourer under the Building and Construction General On-site Award (MA000020) with an award pay floor of about $33.94 to $38.00 per hour (from 1 July 2025), while labour-hire charge rates for the same worker run higher (about $51 to $64 per hour ex-GST); EBA-covered site labourers carry higher floors still.

sources.title: CW1 vs CW4 vs EBA - Construction Rates 2026
sources.whatItMeasured: Private labour-hire vendor's 2026 rate card for CW1 general construction labourer award pay rates and charge rates, referencing Award MA000020 from 1 July 2025

claims.scope: Vendor-published rate card, not an official award document; the pay-floor figures mirror the Building and Construction General On-site Award but are presented by a commercial supplier. It describes pay structure, not employment levels or automation.
claims.refuteNotes: Lens 1 (source real): active labour-hire vendor page, resolves HTTP 200, references the named Award (MA000020) and effective date 1 July 2025. Lens 2 (population fit): CW1 general labourer is this occupation's award classification; the figures are consistent with the Award floor the vendor claims to follow. Lens 3 (in window): 2026 rate card, inside window. Dissent recorded: figures are vendor-stated, so held at trade tier rather than as official award data.

jobAds.notes: The top employers are labour-hire firms (Buildsafe, EIR, HAYS, Synaco), a structural signal that much general labouring is engaged through intermediaries rather than direct hire. No listing mentions AI skills.
